war:hellenic.en:
Typhon's Storm
> "Cronus is asleep. We know it, because if he woke up, we would not be here."
>
> — from the diary of a Talos mechanic

- **Enemy:** **Typhon** — the storm giant with serpent legs, and **the spawn of Echidna** (hydras, chimeras). **Cronus** sleeps silently in the depths
  of Tartarus; Typhon is trying to wake him.
- **Patrons:** Zeus (in the Heavenly Host), **Hephaestus** and the **Cyclopes** (smiths).
- **Giant:** **Talos**.
- **Hero:** **Irini** — a young engineer of the forge of Hephaestus, creator of the automaton phalanxes.
- **Sacrifice:** **Niko the Smith's Apprentice** (1886, "The Storm Wall") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [Typhon's Storm](../campaigns/hellenic.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — storms over the islands; hydras rise from the sea.
  - 1864 — Talos bars the Titans' gate.
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. Typhon rises for the first time: a storm that stands over the sea for weeks.
  - 1890s — "the Storm Wall": automaton phalanxes stand on the shores, Cyclops cannons fire into the sky.
- **Secret:** in the myth Talos has one weak vein — at the heel, stopped with a nail. Medea pulled out that nail and killed Talos.
  The Listeners put their lock **in Talos' nail**. The Greeks find out when Talos staggers in the middle of a battle — and they turn for help
  to **the Sisters of Medea**, the only ones who know this secret.
- **1914:** the front holds. Talos is repaired, but the Greeks do not fully trust the Colchian healers.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the hydra shore → the Storm Wall → Talos' nail → the arrival of the Sisters of Medea → the eye of Typhon.

war:northern.en:
Wolf Winter
- **Enemy:** **Fenrir** and his wolves; in the fjords — the coils of **Jörmungandr**; from the mountains — the **jötnar**.
- **Patrons:** Odin (in the Heavenly Host), **Thor**, **Tyr**, **Heimdall**.
- **Giant:** **the Steel Jotun**.
- **Hero:** **Astrid** — a veteran of the One-Hands of Tyr, who left her hand with a whelp of Fenrir.
- **Sacrifice:** **Eirik the Horn-Keeper** (1879, "Heimdall's Tower") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [Wolf Winter](../campaigns/northern.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1871 — Fenrir's chain breaks. The wolves besiege the towns all winter long.
  - 1880s — following the myth, alchemists make a new chain from "impossible things" — the sound of a cat's footfall, the roots of a mountain.
  - 1902 — Fenrir is bound again. But his wolves remain, and in the fjords Jörmungandr returns.
- **Secret:** the lock was **in the old chain** — a Listener smith cut one link from the inside.
- **1914:** the North holds out, but the winters keep getting longer.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the wolf siege → the search for impossible things → forging the chain → binding Fenrir → the coils of the fjord.

war:celtic.en:
Balor's Eye
- **Enemy:** **Balor** — king of the Fomorians, whose eye burns everything when it opens — and the **Fomorians'** raids from the sea.
- **Patrons:** the Dagda (in the Heavenly Host), **Lugh** (Balor's slayer), **Nuada**, **Goibniu**.
- **Giant:** **the Sling-Colossus of Lugh** — a slinger of stone and iron whose single shot is aimed at Balor's eye.
- **Hero:** **Rowan** — chief of the Marksmen of Lugh, the only one to survive the gaze of Balor's eye.
- **Sacrifice:** **Siofra the Shield-Maker** (1893, "The Eye's Second Night") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [Balor's Eye](../campaigns/celtic.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1871 — an island rises from the sea: Balor's fortress. Every night the eye opens a little.
  - 1880–1900 — the Fomorians plunder the shores; the Smiths of Goibniu forge a shot that will pierce the eye — in three blows, as Goibniu forged the spearhead in the myth.
- **Secret:** the lock was **inside the Marksmen of Lugh**: one of them is a Listener. Rowan has to find out who.
- **1914:** the eye is closed, but the shot has not yet been fired.
- **Campaign idea (4 scenarios):** the Fomorian raid → the traitor marksman → the three-blow shot → the night of the eye.

war:finnish.en:
The Stolen Sun
- **Enemy:** **Louhi** — the mistress of Pohjola, who in the myth stole the sun and moon and hid them in a mountain; **Tuoni** — the river of the dead.
- **Patrons:** Ukko (in the Heavenly Host), **Väinämöinen**, **Ilmarinen**.
- **Giant:** **Ilmarinen's Steam Sun** — a forged sun hung in the sky, which lights the forests until the real one is brought back.
- **Hero:** **Elina** — a singer of Väinämöinen's line, who can open a mountain cliff with her song.
- **Sacrifice:** **Aarne the Furnace-Keeper** (1888, "The Cold Furnace") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The Stolen Sun](../campaigns/finnish.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1871 — the sun goes out over the North. The forests lie in endless twilight.
  - 1878 — Ilmarinen's masters forge the steam sun. It gives light, but no warmth.
- **Secret:** the lock is **in the forged sun** — the thing that keeps the people alive also keeps Louhi's gate open.
- **1914:** the Finns have a choice: put out the steam sun and lock the gate — or keep the light.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** twilight → forging the steam sun → the river of Tuoni → the mountain of Pohjola → the choice (two endings).

war:britain.en:
The War of the Fens
- **Enemy:** **Grendel's mother** and her spawn — monsters that live beneath the fens and meres.
- **Patron:** **Beowulf** (legend).
- **Giant:** **the Fen Fortress-Ship** — a steam ship-giant that crawls through the fens.
- **Hero:** **Wilfred** — commander of the Fen Scouts, the only survivor of the school of the Heirs of Beowulf.
- **Sacrifice:** **Oswin the Torch-Bearer** (1890, "The Hall Door") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The War of the Fens](../campaigns/britain.md)
- **Course of the war:** the fens grow and swallow villages; the monsters attack the halls at night, as in the epic.
- **Secret:** the lock is **beneath the mere, in the mother's hall** — where Beowulf went down in the epic. Wilfred must go down there too.
- **1914:** the fens have stopped growing, but the mother's hall is still open.
- **Campaign idea (4 scenarios):** the night of the hall → the fen march → the fortress-ship → beneath the mere.

war:gaul.en:
The River Monster
- **Enemy:** **the Tarasque** — the armoured dragon of the river, and its spawn.
- **Patron:** **Taranis** (lightning, the wheel).
- **Giant:** **the Wheel of Taranis** — a fortress-engine with a lightning wheel.
- **Hero:** **Éloïse** — a lightning signaller, trained in Iberia.
- **Sacrifice:** **Gilles the Bridge-Warden** (1881, "The Stone Bridge") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The River Monster](../campaigns/gaul.md)
- **Course of the war:** the Tarasque climbs the rivers upstream and wrecks the bridges; the Gauls develop lightning technology together with Iberia.
- **Secret:** the lock is **in the first lightning rifles** — in the joint Iberian-Gaulish work. The two allies eye each other with suspicion.
- **1914:** the Tarasque is wounded and hiding on the riverbed.
- **Campaign idea (4 scenarios):** the broken bridges → the Iberian rifle → suspicion → the wheel on the river.

war:italy.en:
Son of Vulcan
- **Enemy:** **Cacus** — a fire-breathing giant from the caves. In the myth he is **the son of Vulcan**.
- **Patrons:** Jupiter (in the Heavenly Host), **Hercules** (Cacus' slayer), **Vulcan** (the smith).
- **Giant:** **the Colossus of Hercules** — a steel giant with a club.
- **Hero:** **Giulia** — commander of Vulcan's Cannoneers.
- **Sacrifice:** **Matteo the Gun-Boy** (1897, "The Cave Mouth") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [Son of Vulcan](../campaigns/italy.md)
- **Course of the war:** Cacus comes up out of a network of caves and burns the towns; Vulcan's forges fight fire with fire.
- **Tragedy:** Vulcan's smiths are fighting **their own god's son**. Some of them go over to the heretics — "to defend the father's house".
- **Secret:** the lock is **in the forge furnace** — Vulcan's fire itself feeds the gate.
- **1914:** the front is in the caves; half the forges have stopped.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the night of fire → the caves → the traitor smiths → the furnace → the Colossus of Hercules.

war:polianitsy.en:
Morana's Winter
- **Enemy:** **Morana** and the endless winter; **Koschei the Deathless**; the **zmei**.
- **Patrons:** Perun (in the Heavenly Host), **Dazhbog**, the legends of the bogatyrs.
- **Giant:** **the Stone Colossus of Svyatogor** — an old stone giant built in the image of the epic's huge bogatyr, so heavy the earth can barely hold it.
  The winter took the smiths, so the colossus is now driven by women — slowly, but unstoppably.
- **Hero:** **Vasilisa** — the eldest of the polianitsy.
- **Sacrifice:** **Marfa the Bell-Ringer** (1875, "The Zmei's Bridge") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [Morana's Winter](../campaigns/polianitsy.md)
- **Course of the war:** see `06-european-allies.md`. The women fight Morana's winter and try to find out where the men have gone.
- **Secret:** by the fairy tale, Koschei's death is in a needle, the needle in an egg, the egg in a duck, the duck in a hare, the hare in a chest,
  the chest under an oak. Vasilisa learns that **the lock** is there too. And that the men **are not dead** — they are sleeping in Morana's winter.
- **1914:** the lock has been found but not yet broken: Koschei's death and the men's waking are bound together.
- **Campaign idea (6 scenarios):** the empty village → the zmei's bridge → the oak → the chest and the hare → the duck and the egg → the needle (two endings).

war:armenian.en:
The Lakes of the Vishaps
- **Enemy:** **the vishaps** — monsters of the lakes and clouds that swallow the water.
- **Patrons:** Aramazd (in the Heavenly Host), **Vahagn**, **Anahit**, **Astghik**, **Tork Angegh**, **the aralez**.
- **Giant:** **the Colossus of Tork**.
- **Hero:** **Nare** — a keeper of the aralez, whose hound once brought a dead man back to life.
- **Sacrifice:** **Aram the Stonemason** (1883, "The Drained Lake") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The Lakes of the Vishaps](../campaigns/armenian.md)
- **Course of the war:** the vishaps rise from the mountain lakes and drain the valleys of water; the old **vishap stones** lose their power one after another.
- **Secret:** the Listeners put their lock **in a new stone** — one of the vishap stones "restored" in the Age of Sealing. The old stones still
  work; the false stone has to be found among hundreds of real ones.
- **1914:** the false stone has been found. A new wave of vishaps is coming.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the drained valley → the road of the vishap stones → the Colossus of Tork → the false stone → the cloud vishap.

war:oghuz.en:
Descent into the Underworld
- **Enemy:** **Erlik** — lord of the underworld, and the **divs**; **the spawn of Tepegöz**.
- **Patrons:** Tengri (in the Heavenly Host), **Umay**, **Basat**, **Köroğlu**.
- **Giant:** **the Colossus of the Zumrud Bird**.
- **Hero:** **Aydın** — a Hunter of Basat.
- **Sacrifice:** **Kamila the Well-Warden** (1878, "The Well Lid") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [Descent into the Underworld](../campaigns/oghuz.md)
- **Course of the war:** Erlik's gate is a deep well in the earth. The divs come up at night and drag people down into the underworld.
- **Secret:** the lock is **at the bottom of the underworld**. In the fairy tale the hero goes down a well into the underworld, defeats the divs and comes
  back up on the Zumrud bird — feeding the bird **his own flesh** on the way. Aydın goes down the same way, and the Zumrud colossus carries him up. The price — his flesh.
- **1914:** Aydın has come back up, lame, with the lock in his hand. Erlik's well is still open.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the night of the divs → the well → the div of the underworld → the lock → the Zumrud flight.

war:nile.en:
The Thirteenth Hour
> "The night has twelve hours. Each hour has its gate, its guardian and its battle. We count. If we lose count once — morning will not come."
>
> — the words of a timekeeper of the Sun Barque

In our world the **Nile Lands** are the people who live on the banks of the Nile and hold the myths of ancient Egypt as their heritage.
This is not a state of pharaohs — it is a modern people (engineers, sailors, timekeepers) who are returning to the old myth.

- **Enemy:** **Apep** — the huge serpent of chaos, which in the myth attacks the sun barque **every night** to swallow the sun. It cannot be killed —
  only defeated, night after night. Eclipses, sandstorms and earthquakes are Apep's signs. With him, **Apep's serpents**
  come up out of the sand.
- **Patrons:**
  - **Ra** — the sun god (in the Heavenly Host). His **sun barque** sails through the underworld by night and rises again in the morning.
  - **Mehen** — the protector serpent, which coils around Ra in a ring and guards him.
  - **Set** — a strong and ambiguous god, who in the myth stands at the prow of the barque and holds Apep off with a spear. At the front he is respected,
    but not loved.
  - **Ptah** — the craftsman god, patron of all machines.
  - **Isis** — goddess of magic and healing; **Sekhmet** — the lion-headed warrior goddess.
- **Giant:** **the Sun Barque** — a steam fortress-barque forged by Ptah's masters, which crawls over the sand on **wheels shaped like Mehen's coils**.
  At its prow stands a **spear cannon** — in memory of Set's spear. At night it goes out into the desert to meet Apep. Every morning it comes back — so far.
- **Hero:** **Nadia** — timekeeper of the Sun Barque. Her task is to count the hours of the night: the barque must know exactly where it is in each hour of the night.
- **Sacrifice:** **Samir the Helmsman** (1889, "The Barque's Helm") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The Thirteenth Hour](../campaigns/nile.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — serpents come up out of a **sand rift** in the desert (far from the real monuments, deep in the desert).
  - 1863 — the Age of Sealing: Ptah's masters close the rift with a **wax seal** — in the myth a wax figure of Apep was burned to weaken him.
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. The seal melts, and Apep himself rises. That night the sun rose **late**.
  - 1874 — the first sun barque goes out into the desert. It fights Apep every night and comes back every morning.
  - 1890s — **the night war:** the whole front of the Nile Lands fights by night and sleeps by day. The timekeepers are the most respected people of all.
- **Secret — the thirteenth hour:** in the myth the night has **twelve hours**. The sun barque's **clock** was built by coalition engineers in the Age of Sealing
  — and one of them, a Listener, hid a **thirteenth hour** in it. Every night, when the barque counts "twelve", thirteen actually
  pass — and in that one hidden hour the gate is open and Apep grows stronger. That is why the sun rises later every year.
  Nadia notices it when she compares an old Nile clock with the barque's clock.
- **1914:** the thirteenth hour has been found, but the clock cannot be stopped without stopping the barque — and the barque cannot spend even one night
  away from the desert.
- **Campaign idea (6 scenarios — "the hours of the night"):** the sandstorm → the gate of the first hour → Mehen's coil (defending the barque) →
  Set's spear (at Apep's head) → the extra hour (hunting a traitor aboard the barque) → the late morning.
- **As allies (in the builder):** **Timekeepers** (night scouts — they see ambushers), **Spearmen of Set** (monster-hunters
  with a spear cannon), **Warriors of Sekhmet** (heavy assault infantry with lion-headed helmets).
- ⚠️ **Not used:** gathering the parts of Osiris' body (the plot of Age of Mythology), "mummy's curses" and other
  orientalist clichés, the destruction of real monuments (pyramids, temples), living religions.

war:yellow_river.en:
The Flood War
> "My father built the water a wall, and the water knocked the wall down. I dig the water a road. The water follows the road."
>
> — a saying of Yu the Great, as it is repeated at the front

> ⚠️ **Living religions:** in Chinese folk and Daoist tradition many deities are still worshipped today (e.g. the Jade Emperor),
> so they are not used. We use the **legendary hero** (Yu the Great) and the **monsters of myth**. Real dynasties, uprisings and
> 19th-century wars are not used.

The **Yellow River Lands** — a people whose oldest legend is **the Great Flood**. According to the legend the flood lasted for
generations. **Gun** tried to stop it with dams — with **the swelling soil** stolen from heaven — and failed. His son, **Yu the Great**, spent thirteen
years digging **canals** and gave the water a road to the sea. To this people, Yu is the father of engineers.

- **Enemy:**
  - **Xiangliu** — the nine-headed serpent, servant of the lord of the waters. Its blood poisons the land: wherever it is spilled, nothing grows again.
  - **Gonggong** — the rebellious lord of the waters, locked away in the depths, from where he sends floods.
- **Patrons (legend):** **Yu the Great**; **Yinglong** — the winged dragon who taught Yu to cut canals with its tail.
- **The Nine Tripods:** by legend, Yu cast nine bronze tripod cauldrons and pictured every monster on them, so that people would know them.
  In our world these tripods are an **atlas** of every monster — at the front, copies of them are used to learn where a monster's weak spot is.
- **Giant:** **the Colossus of Yinglong** — a winged steam dragon that digs a new riverbed with its tail in a single night.
- **Hero:** **Lin** — a canal engineer who knows every drawing on the Nine Tripods by heart.
- **Sacrifice:** **Wei the Canal-Man** (1892, "The Burst Dike") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The Flood War](../campaigns/yellow_river.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — the rivers flooded in a single night. The spawn of Xiangliu came up out of the water.
  - 1866 — the Age of Sealing: coalition engineers close the gate with a huge **dam** — made of **swelling soil**, a new discovery of alchemy.
    The old masters protest: "this is Gun's way". No one listens to them.
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. The dam did not break — it **grows**. The water goes beneath it, deep into the earth, and the gate widens from below.
  - 1880s — Xiangliu rises. The fields poisoned by its blood have become a strip of the front: nothing grows there, and the trenches must be shored up with stone.
- **Secret — the swelling soil:** the Listeners put their lock **in the material itself**. The swelling soil makes the dam grow higher and opens the gate from below.
  The higher the dam, the wider the gate. The way out is Yu's way: the dam must be **demolished** and canals dug for the water —
  which means first flooding their own fields.
- **1914:** Lin and the old masters demand that the dam be blown up. Many think this is madness. The Colossus of Yinglong is waiting.
- **Campaign idea (6 scenarios):** the flooded field → Xiangliu's blood → the Nine Tripods (finding the monster's weak spot) → the secret of the swelling soil →
  blowing the dam → Yinglong's canal.
- **As allies (in the builder):** **Canal Diggers of Yu** (engineers — digging, draining water), **Tripod Scholars** (show allies the monster's weak
  spot), **Xiangliu Hunters** (volley guns).
- ⚠️ **With Age of Mythology:** the main theme of AoM's Chinese campaign is the toppling of **the pillars of heaven**; Houyi, Fuxi, Nüwa and Shennong are the main
  figures there. We do not use the pillars of heaven or these figures — our war is about floods and canals.

war:japan_isles.en:
The Oni's Treasure
> "A dog, a monkey and a pheasant. One sees, one climbs, one flies. In the fairy tale that was enough."
>
> — the words of an island scout

> ⚠️ **Living religions:** the kami of Shinto (Amaterasu, Susanoo and others) and Buddhist figures are not used. For the same reason
> **Yamata no Orochi** is not used either, since its myth is tied to Susanoo. We use **folk tales and legends**.
> Imperial symbolism (the rising-sun war flag and so on), real wars and the militaristic image of the samurai are not used.

The people of the **Japanese Isles** remember from childhood the tale of **Momotarō** — the boy born from a peach who, with a dog, a monkey and
a pheasant, went to the **island of the oni**, defeated the oni and brought their treasure home. And the legend of **Hidesato**, the archer
who killed the huge centipede, the **Ōmukade**: two arrows glanced off its armour, the third — wet with spittle — struck home.

- **Enemy:**
  - **The oni** — horned, huge evil beings with iron clubs (kin to the Georgian devis).
  - **The Ōmukade** — a giant centipede coiled around a mountain.
  - **The island of the oni** — an island risen from the sea; a gate.
- **Patrons (legend):** **Momotarō** and his three companions; **Hidesato**.
- **Giant:** **the Karakuri Colossus** — a giant of wood and steel, with springs and steam, forged by the masters of the old mechanical puppets (karakuri).
- **Hero:** **Hana** — a master of the bow-cannons, commander of Hidesato's Archers.
- **Sacrifice:** **Kenta the Bridge-Warden** (1885, "The Hundred-Leg Bridge") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The Oni's Treasure](../campaigns/japan_isles.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — the island of the oni rises from the sea; in the mountains the Ōmukade wakes.
  - 1867 — the Age of Sealing: a great expedition lands on the island, defeats the oni and closes the gate — just as in the fairy tale. And, as in the
    fairy tale, it brings **the treasure** home.
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. The gate opens **not on the island, but in the city** — where the treasure was kept.
  - 1880–1900 — the war is at home: the oni beneath the city, the Ōmukade in the mountains. The island still stands in the sea, empty and silent.
- **Secret — the treasure:** the Listeners put their lock **in the oni's treasure**. The spoils of victory were what brought the gate home.
  Hana must take the treasure back to the island — where no one has returned since Momotarō.
- **1914:** the Ōmukade is wounded by two arrows. The third arrow has not yet been fired. The treasure lies packed in a boat.
- **Campaign idea (6 scenarios):** beneath the city → dog, monkey, pheasant (gathering the three scouts) → the Ōmukade's mountain (two arrows) →
  the secret of the treasure → crossing the sea → the island of the oni and the third arrow.
- **As allies (in the builder):** **Hidesato's Archers** (bow-cannon, giant-hunters — the third shot is always the strongest),
  **the Three Companions** (dog — tracking, monkey — climbing cliffs, pheasant — a steam glider for scouting), **Karakuri Soldiers**
  (mechanical puppet-soldiers).
- ⚠️ **With Age of Mythology:** AoM's Japanese campaign has a spider-yokai and Yamata no Orochi, and its plot is about Amaterasu's captivity.
  We do not use these figures or this plot.

war:indian.en:
The Twenty-Fifth Night
> "King, I will tell you a story so the road does not bore you. At the end I will ask you a question. If you know the answer and stay silent — your head will burst."
>
> — the vetala to King Vikram, from the old collection of tales (free rendering)

> ⚠️ **Special care.** The greater part of Indian mythology is **living religion** (Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and others):
> the gods, asuras, rakshasas, nagas, the "Ramayana" and the "Mahabharata" are sacred texts and figures. **None of them is used —
> on either the light or the dark side.** We use only **secular folk tales** — chiefly the **"Twenty-Five Tales of the Vetala"** (Vikram and the vetala),
> a collection of riddle-tales — and general folkloric beings (**bhuta** — ghosts).
> Also not used: colonial history and symbolism (in our world there are no empires in 1914), the theme of partition,
> religious themes and groups, clichés of the "exotic East" (snake charmers, fakirs and so on).
> The people's name is geographic — **the Indian Peninsula** — and does not denote any modern state.

The people of the **Indian Peninsula** have known one old collection of tales since childhood: for twenty-five nights the legendary king **Vikram**
carries the **vetala** down from an old tree on his back — a spirit that lives in a dead body. Every night on the way the vetala tells a story and at the end
asks a riddle. The king answers — and the vetala goes back to the tree. On the twenty-fifth night the king cannot find an answer, falls silent, and then the vetala
tells him the truth: the one who sent him on this errand wanted him dead.

- **Enemy:** **the bhuta** — night ghosts that rise from old battlefields and abandoned places and kill the living
  with fear and cold. On the Night of Opening they came up in their thousands.
- **Ambiguous:** **the vetala** — neither enemy nor ally. It knows a great deal and speaks only in riddles.
- **Patron (legend):** **Vikram** — the legendary king who wins by patience, courage and wisdom — not by force.
- **Giant:** **the Elephant-Fort** — a huge steam war elephant with a whole battery on its back. It frightens off the bhuta with lanterns:
  at night hundreds of fires shine from its belly.
- **Hero:** **Anaya** — captain of the Night Watch, who knows the tale of Vikram by heart and is the only one the vetala will speak to.
- **Sacrifice:** **Ravi the Lantern-Keeper** (1880, "The Lantern Line") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The Twenty-Fifth Night](../campaigns/indian.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — the bhuta rise from old battlefields. At night the villages empty.
  - 1865 — the Age of Sealing: coalition engineers close the gate at the foot of an old **banyan tree**. The vetala sits in the tree and watches everything.
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. The bhuta return, and now the nights grow colder and colder.
  - 1890s — **the lantern war:** the whole front fights with fire by night. The Elephant-Fort walks from village to village.
  - 1913 — an engineer, respected at the front since the Age of Sealing, asks Anaya: "Bring me down the vetala. It will tell me
    where the lock is."
- **Secret — the twenty-fifth night:** Anaya carries the vetala down for twenty-four nights. Every night a riddle, every night an answer, and the vetala goes back to the tree.
  On the twenty-fifth night Anaya falls silent. And the vetala tells her: **the engineer is a Listener**. The lock is at the foot of the tree, and its key is **Anaya's life** —
  that is why he sent her to fetch the vetala: to kill her at the foot of the tree. As in the fairy tale, the traitor seemed a good man.
- **1914:** the engineer has fled; the lock has been found. The vetala has gone back to the tree and is waiting — it says it has one more riddle, at the Wound.
- **Campaign idea (6 scenarios — "the nights"):** the empty village → the lantern line → the Elephant-Fort → the banyan tree (the vetala's first night) →
  the road of riddles (before each scenario, a riddle that grants a bonus) → the twenty-fifth night.
- **As allies (in the builder):** **Lantern-Bearers** (frighten the bhuta with fire, night scouts), **Blades of Vikram** (sworn to the oath
  of patience: they automatically pass Nerve tests), **Elephant-Fort Gunners** (field artillery).
- **The Georgian link:** Georgian fairy tales are full of riddles and stories within stories too. At the front Georgians and Indians compete in riddles.

war:west_african.en:
The Written and the Spoken
> "Paper burns, a hand changes paper. No one can change my memory. My mother taught me, and her mother taught her."
>
> — a storyteller's words to the coalition engineers

> ⚠️ **Special care.**
> - **Africa is not one country or one people.** This war belongs to the peoples of **West Africa**; the peoples of the east, the south and other regions,
>   if we ever write them, will have separate wars of their own.
> - **Not used:** colonialism and slavery (in our world there are no empires), clichés of the "savage", the "primitive" and the "dark continent",
>   **accusations of witchcraft** (still harmful in real life today), living religions (including traditional
>   religions — e.g. the orishas, who are still worshipped today).
> - **Ethiopia** is not used — Trench Crusade already has Abyssinian squads.
> - We use only **folk tales** (Anansi) and **folkloric monsters** (Ninki Nanka). The people are engineers, smiths and
>   soldiers just like every other nation.

Two things unite the peoples of the **West African Lands** in this war: **tales** and **memory**. Everyone knows the tale of **Anansi** —
the spider who bought all the stories: the sky demanded a python, a leopard, hornets and a forest spirit as the price, and Anansi caught all four
**by cunning** — not one by force. These peoples have **storytellers**, who hand history down from generation to generation by heart, word for word.

- **Enemy:**
  - **Ninki Nanka** — the dragon of the mangrove swamps. According to folklore, whoever sees it falls ill and dies.
  - Its **swamp spawn** — scaled creatures from the swamp that attack rivers and harbours.
- **Patron (tale):** **Anansi** — the trickster who defeats the strong with wits.
- **Giant:** **the Colossus of Anansi** — a steel spider-giant that strings a **steel web** over the swamps. It fights Ninki Nanka not by sight but by the web:
  when the web trembles, the monster is there.
- **Hero:** **Adjoa** — an engineer from a family of storytellers. She knows how to build webs — and every one of her grandmother's stories word for word.
- **Sacrifice:** **Kwame the Boatman** (1886, "The Mirror Boat") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The Written and the Spoken](../campaigns/west_african.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — the swamps tremble at night. Fishermen come back sick: "I saw it."
  - 1862 — the Age of Sealing: coalition engineers close the gate with **the Song of the Seal** — words that must be recited at the seal
    every year. The song was written down on paper, and the storytellers memorised it too.
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. Ninki Nanka rises.
  - 1880–1900 — **the war of webs:** the swamps fill with mirrors, periscopes and steel webs. Soldiers never look
    at the monster directly.
- **Secret — one word:** the lock is **in the Song of the Seal**. A Listener changed **one word** in the text written on paper: every year,
  when the song was read from the paper, the seal opened a little. Adjoa notices when she compares her grandmother's spoken version with the paper.
  **Spoken memory defeated the false record.**
- **1914:** now only the spoken song is recited at the seal. Ninki Nanka is weakened, but paper copies were sent all over
  the world — and Adjoa asks: were words changed in the other nations' seals too?
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the fishing village → the line of mirrors → Anansi's four tricks (four sub-missions: wits, not force) →
  the web of the Colossus of Anansi → the Song of the Seal (two versions, one false).
- **As allies (in the builder):** **Net-Weavers** (stop the monster with steel nets), **Mirror Marksmen** (aim at the monster through a periscope
  — no Fear test needed), **Storytellers** (a story that gives allies back their nerve).

war:north_american.en:
Man and Drill
> "The drill doesn't tire, the drill doesn't sleep. The drill can't hear the hammer song. That's why we sing."
>
> — from the song of the Hammer Gang

> ⚠️ **Special care.**
> - **America is two continents and many peoples.** This war belongs to the **North American Forests**. The peoples of Latin America, if we write them,
>   will have a separate war.
> - **The sacred beings and beliefs of Indigenous peoples** (wendigo, thunderbird, skinwalker and others) **are not used** —
>   many communities ask directly that they not be used in entertainment.
> - **Not used:** colonisation, slavery, the civil war, stereotypes of the "Wild West" and of "Indians", any real
>   war or revolution. In our world these states and empires do not exist.
> - We use only the **folk tall tales** — **John Henry**, **Paul Bunyan** — and the invented **fearsome critters**
>   of lumberjack folklore. John Henry is a folk hero of Black Americans, a symbol of the worker's dignity —
>   used only with respect.

The people of the **North American Forests** are a people of railways, mines and forests. Everyone knows two stories:
- **John Henry** — a railway worker who, while a tunnel was being dug, raced a **steam drill** with his hammer and won — and then died of exhaustion.
  He is a symbol of human dignity in the face of the machine.
- **Paul Bunyan** — a giant lumberjack, attended by a blue ox, **Babe**. They say their footprints became lakes.

- **Enemy:** **the fearsome critters** — monsters of the lumberjacks' tales, which now really are coming out of the forest:
  - **the hodag** — a horned, spiny, foul-smelling beast;
  - **the hidebehind** — a creature that always stands behind you, and you never see it;
  - **the snallygaster** — a winged night monster that attacks travellers on the roads.
- **Patrons (tall tales):** **John Henry**, **Paul Bunyan** and **Babe**.
- **Giant:** **the Colossus of Paul Bunyan** — a steam giant lumberjack with an axe, and beside him **Babe** — a blue steel ox-locomotive that
  tramples new roads through the forest.
- **Hero:** **Clara** — leader of the Hammer Gang, whose grandfather worked beside John Henry.
- **Sacrifice:** **Samuel the Tunnel Lamp-Man** (1876, "The Tunnel Collapse") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [Man and Drill](../campaigns/north_american.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — digging a railway tunnel, workers strike a gate of the underworld. The fearsome critters come out of the forest.
  - 1862 — the Age of Sealing: coalition engineers close the tunnel with **a new steam drill** — with a rockfall and a seal.
    The drill was left in the tunnel, "just in case".
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. The sound of steam comes from the tunnel. **The drill is working by itself**.
  - 1880–1900 — **the hammer war:** every night the drill digs deeper and opens the gate wider. The hammer gangs dig new tunnels
    to shore up the seal. In the forest, hidebehinds carry off the night sentries.
- **Secret — the drill:** the lock is **in the drill**. A Listener built it so that on the Night of Opening it would switch itself on and start digging toward the gate.
  The drill can only be stopped by reaching it — that is, **you have to beat the machine with a hammer**, as John Henry did.
- **1914:** Clara's gang is digging toward the drill. Only one wall is left between the two tunnels. In the tale the man won — and died.
- **Campaign idea (6 scenarios):** the tunnel mouth → the hidebehind forest (sentries who cannot look behind them) → Babe's road →
  the night of the snallygaster (defending the railway) → the hammer race (a race against time with the drill) → the last wall.
- **As allies (in the builder):** **the Hammer Gang** (melee + tunnelling), **Lumberjacks** (axes, making wooden cover), **Armoured-Train
  Gunners** (machine-gun from the rails).

war:mexica.en:
The New Fire
> "Fifty-two years were bound into one bundle. Every fire went out. We stood in the dark and watched the stars — would they come down or not.
> The fire was lit. But that fire was not warm."
>
> — the memoir of a fire-runner, 1871

> ⚠️ **Care.**
> - The people of the Valley of Mexico (the Nahua) still live today and speak Nahuatl. Their old gods and calendar are used only **with respect**.
> - **Human sacrifice is not used** — neither in the story nor in the mechanics. The Aztecs are often reduced to that alone; with us
>   they are astronomers, engineers, runners and warriors. In our world blood and sacrifice are the dark side's weapons.
> - **Not used:** the Spanish conquest and colonisation, real revolutions, the stereotype of the "bloodthirsty empire".
> - **With Age of Mythology:** AoM's Aztec campaign has the rivalry of Quetzalcoatl and Tezcatlipoca, the fall of Aztlan, the migration of a people
>   and the obsidian mirror; the goddess Itzpapalotl appears there too. **We use none of these.** Our war is about the tzitzimime and the New Fire.

The **people of the Mexican Valley** believe that the world has already been **destroyed four times**, and that this is the age of **the Fifth Sun**. Every day the sun
wins its road in battle: **Huitzilopochtli**, the warrior of the sun, fights the **stars** every night and defeats them in the morning, with the help of his fiery serpent —
**Xiuhcoatl**.

Two calendars — of 260 days and 365 days — line up once every **52 years**. This is **"the Binding of the Years"**. On that night
every fire goes out, the people wait in the dark and watch whether the **Pleiades** cross the middle of the sky at midnight. If
they do, the **New Fire** is lit on a mountain, and **runners** carry it with torches to every town and every house. If the fire cannot be lit —
the sun will not rise again, and the **tzitzimime** will come down from the sky.

**The last known Binding was in 1507. 1507 + 52 × 7 = 1871.** The Night of Opening fell on the night of the Binding of the Years.

- **Enemy:**
  - **The tzitzimime** — demons of the stars, skeletal winged beings that come down from the sky during eclipses and on the night of the Binding
    to devour people.
  - **The deep tiers of Mictlan** — the nine-tiered world of the dead. Its lords are not evil in themselves —
    but the gate opened **at the bottom of Mictlan**, and the cold rising from below puts out fire.
- **Patrons (in the Heavenly Host):** **Huitzilopochtli** — the warrior of the sun; **Tlaloc** — lord of rain and thunder;
  **Xiuhcoatl** — the fiery serpent, the sun's weapon.
- **Titan:** **the Colossus of the Quinametzin** — according to legend, the **quinametzin** were giants of the age of the First Sun, builders of the oldest
  cities. In our world a colossus of stone and steam is built in their image, and carries a **great fire** in its chest — a fire that
  lights the whole valley when every other fire goes out.
- **Hero:** **Citlali** — an astronomer-engineer. Her name means "star" in Nahuatl; she watches the stars, which are her people's enemies.
- **Sacrifice:** **Mixtli the Runner** (1882, "The Eclipse Torch") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The New Fire](../campaigns/mexica.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — cold rises from a deep rift of Mictlan; in the villages fires go out by themselves.
  - 1864 — the Age of Sealing: coalition engineers close the rift and give the valley's people a new **steam fire-maker** — "for the night of the Binding,
    so the fire will surely light".
  - **1871, the night of the Binding = the Night of Opening.** Every fire goes out. The Pleiades cross the middle of the sky. The fire is lit, the runners spread it across the valley —
    and that same night the tzitzimime come down anyway.
  - 1871–1900 — **the torch war:** the tzitzimime descend at every eclipse. Trenches are built as rings of fire; at night a fire must burn
    in every house.
- **Secret — the old fire:** the lock is **in the fire itself**. In 1871 the Listeners' fire-maker did not light a new fire — it
  lit **an ember brought up from the rift of Mictlan**. The fire blazes, but it is **old**: the years were never really bound, and nothing holds
  the tzitzimime back. The runners themselves carried this fire into every house. The way out is terrible: **every fire in the whole valley must go out
  at once**, they must endure a dark night and light the fire again by hand — the old way.
- **1914:** Citlali knows the secret. Putting out the fire means opening the door to the tzitzimime. **The next Binding is in 1923** — if they do not dare
  before then, the Fifth Sun may never rise again.
- **Campaign idea (6 scenarios):** the darkened village → the ring of torches (the tzitzimime's first descent) → the stair of Mictlan (searching for the secret
  below) → the old ember → putting out every fire (enduring the dark) → the New Fire (the Colossus of the Quinametzin and the runners).
- **As allies (in the builder):** **Fire-Runners** (very fast, with torches — fire, they frighten off the tzitzimime), **Xiuhcoatl Gunners**
  (the fire-serpent cannon — bringing down winged creatures), **Sky-Watchers** (astronomers — they spot winged and ambushing enemies early), **Shields of Tlaloc** (heavy defenders of the rings of fire),
  **Stormers of the Mictlan Stair** (fighters on the stairs of the rift).

war:amazon.en:
The Meeting of the Waters
> "The black water and the white water flow together and do not mix. It has always been so. When they mix — the Boiuna will wake."
>
> — a saying of the river pilots

> ⚠️ **Care.**
> - **Latin America is many peoples and regions.** The Valley of Mexico has its own war (No. 17). This war belongs to **the Amazon basin**. The Andes, the Caribbean
>   and the southern countries, if we write them, will have separate wars (⚠️ in the Andes many traditions are living belief — e.g. Pachamama).
> - We use **widespread folk folklore** (the curupira, the boiuna, the mapinguari), which has become the shared tales of many peoples
>   of the region. The sacred rituals and beliefs of Indigenous communities are not used; Indigenous peoples do not appear as an "exotic" or "savage" backdrop.
> - **Not used:** colonisation, the conquistadors and the myth of El Dorado, **the rubber boom** (1879–1912 — an era of real atrocity), real wars.
> - **The saci** is not used — its folkloric image has a history of racial stereotyping.

The people of the **Amazon Forests and Rivers** are a river people: pilots, fishermen, dock workers and forest experts. They
know two tales best of all:
- **The curupira** — the guardian of the forest, whose **feet point backwards**: its tracks always lead the opposite way, and whoever harms
  the forest loses their way.
- **The boiuna** — a huge black river serpent that sleeps in deep waters and drags boats to the bottom.

Near the Amazon two great rivers — **the black** and **the white** — flow side by side and for kilometres **do not mix**. This is a real natural
phenomenon. In our world that line is a **seal**: the Boiuna sleeps beneath it.

- **Enemy:**
  - **The Boiuna** — the black river serpent.
  - **The mapinguari** — a huge, shaggy forest giant, one-eyed, with a mouth on its belly; in the tales its roar silences the forest.
  - Their spawn come up out of the forest and the river.
- **Patrons (tales):** **the curupira** — by cunning, not force; **the boitatá** — a fire serpent that protects the fields from fire-raisers.
- **Giant:** **the Colossus of the Curupira** — a steam forest giant with **backward feet**. Its tracks always lead the opposite way,
  and the mapinguari's spawn always follow its trail wrongly.
- **Hero:** **Lúcia** — a river pilot who knows the line between the black and white waters with her eyes shut.
- **Sacrifice:** **Joaquim the Pilot** (1889, "The Mad Pilot") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The Meeting of the Waters](../campaigns/amazon.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — the mapinguari's roar is heard in the forest. Boats disappear.
  - 1866 — the Age of Sealing: coalition engineers build a **measuring station** on the line where the waters meet — a steam barge that watches the line
    and powers the riverside towns with electricity. The people like it: for the first time there is light at night.
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. The Boiuna wakes — only halfway, so far.
  - 1880–1900 — **the river war:** armoured steamboats fight the Boiuna's spawn; in the forest the Colossus of the Curupira
    leads the mapinguari's spawn astray.
- **Secret — the line is moving:** the lock is **in the measuring station**. Every night it pumps a little **black water into the white**. The line moves
  from year to year — so slowly that no one notices, except Lúcia, who has known the line since childhood. When the waters mix completely, the Boiuna
  will wake fully. The station must be sunk — and the riverside towns will be left in the dark again.
- **1914:** Lúcia has proved that the line is moving. The towns oppose sinking the station. The Boiuna breathes deeply.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the lost boat → the curupira's tracks (misleading the enemy) → the mapinguari's roar → the line is moving
  (a measuring mission on the river) → sinking the station.
- **As allies (in the builder):** **River Pilots** (boat scouts, swift on water), **Curupira Scouts** (false tracks — ambush
  and misleading the enemy), **Mapinguari Hunters** (harpoon-guns, giant-hunters).

war:andes.en:
The Woven Bridge
> "A steel bridge stands a hundred years. A grass bridge — one year. That is why we weave the grass bridge together every year. The bridge doesn't bind us — the weaving does."
>
> — the words of a mountain village elder

> ⚠️ **Special care.**
> - Many traditions of the Andes are **still living belief** (Pachamama — mother earth, the apus — spirits of the mountains, the belief in three worlds). **They are not
>   used** — neither as characters nor as enemies.
> - **Not used:** the Spanish conquest, the history of the silver mines, the myth of the "lost city of gold", historical uprisings and their
>   symbols, the destruction of old cities and monuments.
> - We use: the **old legend** of stone giants, **folk craft** (hanging bridges woven of grass rope, which communities still weave together today —
>   only with respect), the sling and the running messengers.

The people of the **Andean Highlands** are a people of mountains, gorges and bridges. Here the gorges are so deep that the villages are linked only by **bridges**
— hanging bridges **woven of grass rope**. A grass bridge does not last long, so **every year** the villages on both banks
gather, weave the rope and hang the bridge anew.

An old legend says that the maker of the world **first made giants of stone**. The giants proved rebellious, and the maker
destroyed them with a flood and turned them to stone. Only after that did he make people — smaller ones.

- **Enemy:** **the giants of the first creation** — stone giants that **stood up** from the mountainsides on the Night of Opening. They are slow,
  nearly impenetrable, and they wreck bridges: the descendants of the rebels hate the ties between people.
  With them come **the stone spawn**, small stone creatures that rise from their fragments.
- **Patrons:** we do not use gods (see above). This people's strength is in **the community**: in the weaving of the bridge, in the running **messengers** who pass news
  to each other along the mountain roads, and in the **sling** — the old mountain weapon.
- **Giant:** **the Condor Colossus** — a winged steam giant that flies over the gorges and carries bridges from bank to bank.
- **Hero:** **Kusi** — from a family of bridge-weavers, the only one of her generation who knows every knot of the old weaving.
- **Sacrifice:** **Ilari the Runner** (1890, "The Last Message") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The Woven Bridge](../campaigns/andes.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — stones move on the mountainsides. Bridges snap at night.
  - 1866 — the Age of Sealing: over the deepest gorge — where the gate opened — coalition engineers build a **steel bridge**. "It will stand
    a hundred years — you won't need to weave the grass bridge any more." For one year, then a second, the people do not gather to weave.
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. The steel bridge stands. Stone giants climb up from the bottom of the gorge.
  - 1880–1900 — **the war of the bridges:** the giants walk from gorge to gorge and wreck the bridges; the villages are cut off from each other. The messengers run
    along the mountain paths, the slingers fight the stone spawn from the cliffs.
- **Secret — the weaving:** in the old way the seal **was not the bridge — it was the weaving**: the yearly gathering, when the people of both banks wove one rope together.
  The Listeners' steel bridge ended that gathering — and the seal weakened year by year. The lock is **in the steel bridge**: it joins the two banks
  of the gorge, but not the people. Kusi demands that the steel bridge be cut down and that every village weave a grass bridge together again —
  at the edge of the gorge, where the giants come up.
- **1914:** the steel bridge has been cut down. The weaving has begun. The villages gather on both banks — and the stone giants feel it.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the fallen bridge → the messengers' road (bringing word to cut-off villages) → the slingers' cliff →
  cutting down the steel bridge → the night of weaving (holding out until the bridge is finished; the Condor Colossus carries the end of the rope to the far bank).
- **As allies (in the builder):** **Bridge-Weavers** (engineers — rope bridges and barriers), **Chaski Runners** (runners — carry orders and news
  far), **Andean Slingers** (stones hurled from the cliffs — the advantage of height).
- **The Georgian link:** in the mountains of the Caucasus too, gorges divide the villages. At the front Georgian and Andean highlanders tell each other mountain stories.

war:caribbean.en:
The Lighthouse Alphabet
> "Every night the lighthouse says the same thing: short, short, long. I thought it was talking to the ships."
>
> — a letter from a lighthouse keeper's daughter

> ⚠️ **Special care.**
> - **The Caribbean Isles are many peoples, languages and cultures.** In this war they stand on the islands' common front, each with its own shore.
> - **Not used:** slavery, plantations, colonisation, the romanticisation of pirates, the sacred beings of the Taíno (including the hurricane
>   deity), real hurricanes and disasters.
> - **Living religions are not used:** Vodou, Santería, Obeah, Rastafari and others. **"Zombies" are not used** — they are a distorted
>   stereotype of Vodou belief. Also not used: the **soucouyant** and other "witch-woman" beings (the theme of witchcraft accusations).
> - We use only the **folk tales of nature's guardians** (Papa Bois — father of the forest, Mama Dlo — mother of the river) and a **monster of sea
>   folklore** (the Lusca). The people are sailors, fishermen, lighthouse keepers, telegraphists and engineers.

In the sea of the **Caribbean Isles** there are **blue holes** — deep, round, dark blue wells sunk into the seabed. This is a real natural
phenomenon. In the fishermen's tales the **Lusca** lives in them — half shark, half octopus, a monster that drags boats down into the hole.
In our world the blue holes are **small gates** — hundreds of them, all over the sea.

- **Enemy:**
  - **The Lusca** — the monster of the blue holes; at night its tentacles rise to the surface and attack boats, jetties and shore villages.
  - **The Lusca's spawn** — small tentacled creatures that come up out of the holes and onto the shore.
- **Patrons (tales):**
  - **Papa Bois** — the father of the forest, an old guardian with hoofed feet, who protects the animals and the trees.
  - **Mama Dlo** — the mother of the river, half woman, half serpent, guardian of rivers and springs.
- **Giant:** **the Colossus of Papa Dlo** — a huge steam sea serpent that coils around the blue holes and grips the Lusca's tentacles.
- **Hero:** **Marisol** — a lighthouse keeper's daughter and telegraphist; the only one who can read an alphabet in the lighthouse's flashes.
- **Sacrifice:** **Eduardo the Lighthouse-Keeper** (1889, "The Light Put Out") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The Lighthouse Alphabet](../campaigns/caribbean.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — tentacles rise from the blue holes. The fishermen stop going to sea at night.
  - 1865 — the Age of Sealing: coalition engineers build a **chain of lighthouses** across the islands: a powerful light shines on the blue holes, and the Lusca
    flees the light. One after another the holes "close".
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. The lighthouses are lit — and the Lusca rises anyway.
  - 1880–1900 — **the lighthouse war:** there is war on every island at night; at sea armoured steamboats and harpoon fishermen fight,
    and on the shore — trenches in the sand.
- **Secret — the lighthouse alphabet:** the lock is **in the lighthouses' flashing**. Every lighthouse flashes — that is normal, it is how ships tell
  which lighthouse is which. But the Listeners' lighthouses all share one and the same **signal** — short, short, long — which is meant not for ships
  but for **the seabed**. The light frightens the Lusca, but the flashing **calls** it — exactly where the ships pass.
  Marisol notices when she writes the flashing down in telegraph code.
- **1914:** the lighthouses' flashing must be changed — all together, on one night. That night the sea will be dark.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the night fishermen → the blue hole (defending the boats) → the lighthouse alphabet (taking down the code in the middle of the fighting) →
  the Colossus of Papa Dlo → the night of the dark sea (changing every lighthouse at once).
- **As allies (in the builder):** **Lighthouse Keepers** (lanterns and signal rockets — night vision, lighting up allies), **Harpoon
  Fishers** (monster-hunters, swift on water), **Papa Bois Scouts** (ambush in the forest).

war:oceania.en:
Stars and Compass
> "The compass says — north. The swell says something else. The star says the same as the swell. I trust two, not one."
>
> — the words of a canoe wayfinder

> ⚠️ **Special care.**
> - **Oceania** is many peoples on thousands of islands (Polynesia, Melanesia, Micronesia), each with their own languages and traditions.
> - The gods and ancestral beings of these peoples **are still living belief and sacred knowledge** (including some that popular culture
>   has already used, causing protest). **None of them is used** — neither as patron nor as enemy. Water-guardian beings,
>   which many communities regard as protectors, **are not shown as evil**. Tattoo designs and war dances are not used.
> - The traditions of the Indigenous peoples of **Australia** are sacred and often secret knowledge — they are **not part of** this war.
> - **Not used:** colonisation, the forced recruitment of labourers (at the end of the 19th century — exactly our era), real tsunamis and disasters.
> - **That is why this is the only war in which the enemy does not come from these peoples' mythology.** The enemy is **Hell's fleet** — the dark side
>   of our world. The people's strength is **the knowledge of navigation**: sailing by stars, swells and stick charts — only with respect.

The peoples of the **Isles of Oceania** have been ocean navigators since ancient times. They crossed the vast ocean by **the stars**, **the rhythm of the
swells**, by birds and clouds, and on some islands they recorded the direction of the swells on **charts of sticks and shells**.
This knowledge is handed down from generation to generation.

In the depths of the ocean — in the world's **deepest trench** — a gate of Hell opened.

- **Enemy:** **Leviathan's fleet** — the legions of **Leviathan**, Hell's great admiral: black steam submarines, deep-water
  demons and monsters of the deep that rise from the trench and cut the islands off from each other.
- **Patrons:** we do not use gods (see above). This people's strength is **knowledge** and **each other**: the islands are linked to each other by canoe.
- **Giant:** **the Canoe of the Stars** — a twin-hulled steam fortress-canoe with a whole harbour between its two hulls. It has no helm —
  the wayfinders steer it by the stars.
- **Hero:** **Leilani** — a wayfinder who learned to read the swells from her grandmother.
- **Sacrifice:** **Tui the Lantern-Man** (1897, "The Lit Boat") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [Stars and Compass](../campaigns/oceania.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — unknown ships rise from the deep ocean. The fish disappear.
  - 1867 — the Age of Sealing: the coalition closes the trench with a sunken seal and gives the islands **steamships** and **compasses**:
    "you won't need the stars any more". The young stop learning the old knowledge.
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. Leviathan's fleet rises.
  - 1880–1900 — **the war of the islands:** the ships carrying troops and supplies from island to island vanish one after another.
- **Secret — the compass:** the lock is **in the compasses**. The needle of every coalition compass is magnetised with underworld iron: on the open ocean
  it points not north but **to the trench** — almost imperceptibly, a little more each day. Every convoy that sails by compass ends up at the trench,
  at Leviathan's fleet. Leilani notices when she compares the stars and the swells with the compass.
- **1914:** every compass has been thrown into the sea. Now only the wayfinders guide the fleet — and there are very few of them. The old knowledge
  must be taught to the young quickly.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the lost convoy → reading the swells (navigating around the enemy fleet) → the secret of the compass →
  the Canoe of the Stars → above the trench (restoring the seal from the surface).
- **As allies (in the builder):** **Wayfinders** (scouts — they bring the warband out in an unexpected place), **Canoe Raiders** (fast
  landings from twin-hulled canoes), **Reef Wardens** (masters of fighting on the coral reefs — they stop anything coming from the sea).
- **The Georgian link:** many compasses were replaced at the Colchian Sea Gate too. When they heard Oceania's story, the Colchian sailors began
  checking their compasses as well.

war:central_african.en:
The Returned Sceptre
> "He was born talking, standing on his feet, with the sceptre in his hand. We never gave that sceptre to anyone. It was taken — 'for study'."
>
> — a storyteller of a forest village

The people of the **Central African Forests** know **the epic of Mwindo** — a great oral epic that storytellers used to tell for days. Mwindo
was born speaking and walking, holding a **magic sceptre** (a flywhisk of animal tail) that could bring the dead to life. He
went down into the underworld, withstood the tricks of the lord of the underworld, defeated the great dragon **Kirimu**, and was helped by the lightning — **Nkuba**.

- **Enemy:** **Kirimu** and its spawn — dragons risen from the deep swamps of the forest; after them come the **servants of the
  underworld**, who carry people off into the depths of the forest.
- **Patrons (epic):** **Mwindo** — the hero who returns from the underworld; **Nkuba** — the lightning, his ally.
- **Giant:** **the Colossus of Nkuba** — a giant of steam and lightning that hurls thunderbolts over the forest.
- **Hero:** **Maisha** — a daughter of a family of storytellers, and a telegraph engineer.
- **Sacrifice:** **Bakari the Porter** (1910, "The Last Load") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The Returned Sceptre](../campaigns/central_african.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — dragons rise from the forest swamps; villages vanish.
  - 1864 — the Age of Sealing: coalition engineers close the gate. The people show them the old **sceptre of Mwindo** — the village's treasure, with which
    the seal was bound. The engineers take the sceptre to **the coalition's repository** "for study and safekeeping".
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. Kirimu rises.
- **Secret — the taken sceptre:** the lock is **the sceptre's absence**. The seal was bound with the sceptre every year; once the sceptre was taken, no one
  bound the seal any more. The Listener engineer knew what he was taking. Maisha learns that the sceptre stands in the repository, in a glass case, labelled "unknown object".
- **1914:** Maisha has brought the sceptre back to the village. The seal is being bound again — but the people are asking about the coalition's other objects "in safekeeping".
  ⚠️ This is a story of **return** — from an invented coalition repository, without naming any real country or museum.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the lost village → Kirimu's swamp → the repository (finding the sceptre) → the road home → binding the seal.
- **As allies (in the builder):** **Nkuba's Thunder Gunners**, **Forest Trackers** (ambush), **Storyteller-Telegraphists** (communications, orders).

war:southern_african.en:
The Swallowed Fortress
> "It swallowed everything — people, cattle, houses. One woman was left. Her son, who was born fully grown, cut the monster's
> belly open from inside — and everyone came out alive."
>
> — a mountain tale, as it is told at the front

The tales of the people of the **Southern African Mountains** tell of **Kammapa** — a monster that swallowed an entire people — and **Litaolane**, a boy
who was fully grown the moment he was born: he let the monster swallow him and cut its belly open from inside, and the swallowed people
came out alive.

- **Enemy:** **Kammapa** — a mountain-sized monster that swallows everything — people, livestock, fortifications.
- **Patron (tale):** **Litaolane**.
- **Giant:** **the Colossus of Litaolane** — a steam giant "great from birth", with a huge saw-blade on its arm.
- **Hero:** **Lerato** — commander of the Mountain Riflemen.
- **Sacrifice:** **Naledi the Pump-Keeper** (1871, "The Cooled Walls") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The Swallowed Fortress](../campaigns/southern_african.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — Kammapa comes up out of a mountain valley. In a single night two villages vanish — without a trace.
  - 1866 — the Age of Sealing: the coalition builds a huge **steel fortress** over the gate. The fortress presses down on the gate with its weight.
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. Kammapa rises and **swallows the fortress whole** — garrison and all.
- **Secret — the hollow fortress:** the lock is **in the fortress**. The Listeners built it hollow and light inside — made to be swallowed.
  Now the fortress is inside the monster, and its steel has become the gate's prop: while the fortress is in Kammapa's belly, the gate is open. And, as in the
  fairy tale, the garrison inside is **alive** — its signals are heard from the belly at night.
- **1914:** Lerato's squad chooses the fairy tale's way: the monster must swallow **them** too, so they can cut their way out and bring out the fortress and its people.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the empty village → signals from the belly → being swallowed (willingly) → the fortress inside the monster → cutting out from inside.
- **As allies (in the builder):** **Mountain Riflemen** (shooting from the cliffs), **Saw-Blades** (cutters of the monster's armour, melee), **Mounted
  Scouts** (mountain horses).

war:great_lakes.en:
Silence
> "When the Digger goes down, everyone must fall silent. One shout — and it will run again."
>
> — from an old story of the Great Lakes Lands

In the old legend of the people of the **Great Lakes Lands**, the first man, **Kintu**, married **Nambi**, a daughter of the sky, and with them, against
their will, came Nambi's brother **Walumbe** — **Death**. When Walumbe began killing people, the sky sent another brother, **Kayikuuzi**,
to catch him. Kayikuuzi dug into the earth, and Walumbe hid in the pits. Kayikuuzi told the people: **"Be silent, whatever
you see."** The children saw Walumbe, cried out — and he fled into the earth. That is why death remained on the earth.

> ⚠️ This legend is the national heritage of this people; some of its characters belong to traditional belief too. We use only **the story** —
> without rituals or real sacred places.

- **Enemy:** **Walumbe** — Death, which hides beneath the earth, in pits, and its **shadows**, which come up out of the pits.
- **Patron (legend):** **Kayikuuzi** — the Digger, who hunts Death.
- **Giant:** **the Digger Colossus** — a steam giant with drill hands, which digs the ground quietly and slowly.
- **Hero:** **Nakato** — commander of the Diggers.
- **Sacrifice:** **Okello the Deaf Digger** (1898, "The Bottom of the Pit") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [Silence](../campaigns/great_lakes.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — pits appear on the lakeshores; at night shadows come up out of them.
  - 1866 — the Age of Sealing: the coalition equips the front with **steam sirens** — "for alarms": when a shadow appears, the siren screams.
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. Walumbe rises.
  - 1880–1900 — **the Diggers' war:** the squads dig pits and hunt Walumbe. Every time they get close, he vanishes.
- **Secret — the sirens:** the lock is **in the sirens**. Every alarm is the cry the children gave in the legend: it warns Walumbe,
  and he flees into the earth. The siren always screams just when the Diggers are closest. Nakato proves it from the records.
- **1914:** the front demands that for one night **every siren, every gun and every voice** fall silent while the Diggers go down. That night
  no one fires — not even when the shadows attack.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the pits → the night of the siren → the records → the silent front (a scenario where shooting is forbidden) → the bottom of the pit.
- **As allies (in the builder):** **the Diggers** (tunnels, digging), **Silent Warriors** (melee, without a sound — ambush), **Lake Boatmen**.

war:north_african.en:
False Water
> "At night the pump roars as if a river were flowing. But in the khettara the water gets less every year. Who is lying to us — the pump, or our ears?"
>
> — the words of a mountain village digger

> ⚠️ **Special care.**
> - The peoples of North Africa — the **Amazigh** and **Arabic-speaking** peoples — today live largely in the context of a living religion.
>   So **jinn, ghouls and other beings of religious folklore are not used**, just as living religion is not.
> - **Carthage and the Phoenician deities are not used** (see the rules of political correctness — this heritage belongs to living peoples).
> - **Not used:** colonisation (exactly in our era — with real wars), clichés of "Barbary pirates", "desert raiders" and other
>   orientalist clichés, the exoticisation of the Tuareg.
> - **As in Oceania, the enemy here also comes from the dark side of our world** — from a legion of Hell. The people's strength is their **real knowledge**:
>   the **khettaras** (underground irrigation channels), the **agadirs** (communal fortified granaries) and the community working together — only with respect.

The peoples of the **Atlas and Sahara Lands** are peoples of the mountains and the desert. For centuries they carried water by **khettara** — underground
channels dug by hand from the foot of the mountains to the oasis — and kept their harvest in **agadirs** — fortified granaries shared by the whole
village. Every year the whole village cleans the khettara together.

- **Enemy:** **the legions of Crocell** — the Duke of Hell **Crocell** is, in the old lists, the one who "makes the sound of a river where there is no
  water". His legions create mirages in the desert, lure caravans with the sound of false water and dry out the wells. With them come
  **the sand spawn**, which drink water wherever they find it.
- **Patrons:** we do not use gods or religious beings (see above). This people's strength is **the knowledge of water** and **the community**.
- **Giant:** **the Agadir Colossus** — a walking fortress-granary that carries water and grain to besieged villages. It is the opposite of the Grand
  Harness: the Grand Harness gathers captives, the agadir hands out supplies.
- **Hero:** **Tileli** — daughter of a khettara digger. Her name means "freedom" in Amazigh.
- **Sacrifice:** **Amastan the Caravan Guide** (1894, "The Mirage Trap") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [False Water](../campaigns/north_african.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — mirages multiply in the desert; caravans vanish. The water in the wells disappears at night.
  - 1866 — the Age of Sealing: the coalition closes the gate and gives the villages **deep steam pumps**: "you won't need to clean the khettaras any more —
    the pump will bring the water up by itself". Many villages stop cleaning their khettara.
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. The legions of Crocell rise.
  - 1880–1900 — **the water war:** villages and oases are under siege; the Agadir Colossus walks from siege to siege.
- **Secret — the false water:** the lock is **in the pumps**. The pumps draw up the deep water — and with it they pull the groundwater **toward the gate**.
  The roar in the pumps that sounds like a river is Crocell's voice. The khettaras are drying up because the pumps are drinking their water. Tileli notices
  when she compares the water level in the khettara with the pump's roar at night.
- **1914:** the villages are switching off the pumps and cleaning the khettaras together. It is slow work — and the legions attack while it goes on.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the lost caravan (the mirage trap) → the besieged agadir → the night of the pump (the secret of the sound) →
  cleaning the khettara (defending the diggers below ground and above) → the march of the Agadir Colossus.
- **As allies (in the builder):** **Khettara Diggers** (tunnels, bringing water), **Caravan Guards** (trust no mirage — they see ambushes),
  **Agadir Guards** (shield wall — defending a stronghold).

war:central_asian.en:
The White Div's Dust
> "The div blinded the king's army. Rostam killed the White Div in its cave and opened the army's eyes with its blood.
> And we entrusted our eyes to goggles."
>
> — the words of a mountain guide

> ⚠️ **Care.**
> - Central Asia is many peoples — Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Uzbeks, Turkmen, Tajiks and others. In this war they stand on one front.
> - **From the epics we take only the fights with monsters.** The Iran–Turan wars of the "Shahnameh" and the battles of other epics against real peoples
>   (e.g. the wars of "Manas" and "Alpamysh") **are not used** — these peoples are still each other's neighbours today.
> - **Not used:** living religions and rituals (including the modern belief in Tengri), demon-women (the theme of witchcraft accusations),
>   the region's 19th-century conquest and "the Great Game" — this was happening exactly in our era.

The peoples of the **Central Asian Mountains and Steppes** are peoples of the mountains, the oases and the horse. Everyone knows two stories:
- **Rostam**, hero of the **"Shahnameh"**, and his **Seven Labours** — crossing the desert, the lion, the dragon, and finally killing **the White Div** in a mountain
  cave. The divs had blinded the king's army; Rostam opened the army's eyes with the White Div's blood. Rostam wore a tiger's skin and carried a bull-headed
  mace, and his horse was **Rakhsh**.
- **The tulpar** — the winged horse of the steppe peoples, which carries heroes faster than the wind.

- **The Georgian link:** the "Shahnameh" was also translated into Georgian, as the **"Rostomiani"**, and a hero clad in a tiger's skin is familiar to the Georgian reader
  — from **"The Knight in the Panther's Skin"**. The div and the Georgian **devi** are words from one root. At the front the Georgians count Rostam as "one of ours".
- **Enemy:** **the White Div** and **the divs** — huge beings risen from the mountain caves, who command **dust storms**
  and blind their enemies.
- **Patrons (epic):** **Rostam** and **Rakhsh**; **the tulpar**.
- **Giant:** **the Tulpar Colossus** — a winged steam horse-giant that flies above the dust storm.
- **Hero:** **Aigerim** — a steppe scout who walks through a dust storm without goggles.
- **Sacrifice:** **Bauyrzhan the Scout** (1885, "The Blind Column") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The White Div's Dust](../campaigns/central_asian.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — dust storms come down from the mountains and blind the caravans. Inside the storm, divs walk.
  - 1866 — the Age of Sealing: the coalition closes the mountain gate and equips the front with **dust goggles** — "for seeing in the storm".
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. The White Div rises.
  - 1880–1900 — **the dust war:** the army fights in the storm, wearing goggles — and every time the divs appear without warning, as if they were invisible.
- **Secret — the goggles:** the lock is **in the goggles' glass**. It is cast from underworld sand: it keeps out the dust — and **it does not show
  the divs either**. In the epic the divs blinded the army; with us the army put on blind eyes of its own free will. Aigerim notices when
  she takes off her goggles in the storm — and sees the divs.
- **1914:** the army is taking off its goggles. Fighting with unprotected eyes in a dust storm is terrible — but now the divs can be seen. As in the epic,
  the White Div's blood, they say, will heal eyes damaged by the goggles.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the blind caravan → the dust storm (a visibility mechanic) → the secret of the goggles → the Tulpar Colossus →
  the White Div's cave.
- **As allies (in the builder):** **Heirs of Rostam** (heavy mace-fighters — div-hunters), **Tulpar Riders** (fast cavalry),
  **Mountain Guides** (climbing cliffs, seeing through the dust).

war:gulf.en:
The Sleeping Islands
> "In the tale the sailors went ashore on an island and lit a fire. The island opened its eye and sank into the sea. We built a coal depot there."
>
> — a sailor's words

> ⚠️ **The most sensitive region — special care.**
> - Three living world religions and many other beliefs were born here. **No religion, sacred figure, sacred place or religious
>   being (including the jinn) is used.**
> - **Not used:** real states, borders and conflicts; the wars, genocides and deportations of the early 20th century
>   (exactly in our era); Sumer, Babylon and Assyria (see the rules of political correctness); disputed names (so we simply call the sea **"the Gulf"**).
> - **Trench Crusade's gate of Hell is in exactly this region** — with us there is no main gate here at all. This people is on the light side,
>   just like all the others. TC's alchemists, its "House of Wisdom" and the like are not used.
> - **Orientalist clichés are not used:** harems, flying carpets, "thieves", exotic bazaars.
> - We use only the **tales of Sindbad the Sailor** — secular adventure stories of the sea: the island that turned out to be an animal, and
>   the huge bird, the **roc** — and the real seafaring knowledge of these shores: the **dhow** (the sailing ship), the **pearl divers**.

The people of the **Gulf and Red Sea Coasts** are a people of seafarers, merchants and pearl divers. Everyone knows the tales of **Sindbad**:
on his first voyage his ship stopped at a small island. The sailors went ashore and lit a fire —
and **the island woke up**: it was a huge sea animal with earth and trees growing on its back. It dived into the sea and took the sailors with it.

- **Enemy:** **the sleeping islands** — huge sea animals that rose from the gate, sleep on the surface for years and look like
  islands. When they wake they destroy ships and harbours. **Sea spawn** climb down from their backs.
- **Patrons:** we do not use gods or religious beings. This people's strength is **the knowledge of the sea**: winds, currents, divers' lungs.
- **Giant:** **the Roc Colossus** — a winged steam giant built in the image of the tale's huge bird, which drops boulders from
  above — just as the roc dropped stones on the ship in the tale.
- **Hero:** **Laila** — a dhow helmswoman and a pearl diver's daughter; she knows every current of the Gulf by heart.
- **Sacrifice:** **Salem the Diver** (1896, "The Deep Breath") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [The Sleeping Islands](../campaigns/gulf.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — new, unknown islands appear in the Gulf. Some change place at night.
  - 1866 — the Age of Sealing: the coalition closes the gate and builds **coal depots for steamships** on the new islands:
    "you won't need the sailing dhows any more".
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. The depots' furnaces are burning.
  - 1880–1900 — **the war of the islands:** one after another the islands wake and drag ships, depots and harbours into the sea.
- **Secret — fire on the back:** the lock is **in the coal depots**. The Listeners knew exactly that these islands were animals, and
  deliberately built the depots on their backs. The heat of the furnaces wakes the animals, just as in the tale — one after another, year after year.
  Laila notices when she sees that the islands wake only after the depots are built.
- **1914:** the depots' furnaces are being put out. The fleet is going back to **sail** — to the dhows — and the divers go down beneath the sleeping islands
  to find out which is an animal and which a real island.
- **Campaign idea (5 scenarios):** the new island → the waking (defending the harbour) → the divers' descent (which island is alive?) →
  putting out the furnaces → the Roc Colossus' boulders.
- **As allies (in the builder):** **Dhow Sailors** (climbing aboard and boarding — melee), **Pearl Divers** (moving underwater,
  ambush), **Coast Gunners** (cannons against sea monsters).

war:sea_islands.en:
False Moons
> "In the tale there were seven moons in the sky, and the sea serpent swallowed six. At every eclipse the people protect the seventh — with pots, gongs and shouting.
> And we lit new moons in the sky."
>
> — the words of an island gong-player

> ⚠️ **Care.**
> - The region is many peoples and cultures, with many **living religions** (Buddhism, Islam, Hinduism, Christianity, local beliefs and
>   spirit veneration). **No religious being is used**, including the naga and the garuda (in some countries also a state symbol).
> - **Not used:** "witch-woman" beings (the theme of witchcraft accusations), colonial wars (some happened exactly in our era) and
>   the wars and crimes of the 20th century.
> - We use the **folk tale** of the **Bakunawa** — the sea serpent that swallows the moon — and the region's real **gong culture**:
>   during a lunar eclipse the people make a din to force the serpent to give back the moon.

The peoples of the **Southeast Asian Isles and Shores** are peoples of the sea, of bronze and of **gongs**. By the tale, the sky once shone with
**seven moons**, and a huge serpent risen from the sea — the **Bakunawa** — swallowed six. To save the last moon
the people beat pots, gongs and drums at every eclipse until the serpent spits the moon back out.

**Unlike the war of the Great Lakes (No. 24)** — where the enemy is defeated by **silence** — here the enemy is defeated by **noise**.

- **Enemy:** **the Bakunawa** — a huge sea serpent-dragon that climbs from the sea toward the sky at night and swallows the light; its **spawn**
  come out onto the shores.
- **Patrons:** we do not use religious beings. This people's strength is **sound** — gongs, drums and shouting together — and **the knowledge of the sea**.
- **Giant:** **the Gong Colossus** — a walking bronze giant whose chest is one huge gong. Its sound shakes the sea and drives the Bakunawa
  back.
- **Hero:** **Ligaya** — a gong-player and electrician; her name means "joy".
- **Sacrifice:** **Danilo the Gong-Player** (1895, "The Last Gong") — see `11-sacrifices.md`. **Campaign:** [False Moons](../campaigns/sea_islands.md)
- **Course of the war:**
  - 1847 — the Bakunawa rises from the sea. Eclipses become more frequent.
  - 1866 — the Age of Sealing: the coalition closes the gate and builds **seven electric lighthouse towers** on the islands — "new moons" that
    light the sea at night. The gongs, they say, "you won't need any more".
  - 1871 — the Night of Opening. The Bakunawa rises and swallows the first "new moon".
  - 1880–1910 — **the war of the moons:** the serpent swallows the towers one after another. After every light it swallows it grows bigger and climbs higher
    toward the sky.
